content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed an operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB), specifically focusing on Module 6, which addresses TB and its comorbidities, including mental health conditions. This handbook is available in both electronic and print formats and is intended to guide countries in implementing WHO recommendations for TB care, particularly in the context of comorbidities and health-related risk factors. The handbook emphasizes the importance of integrated, patient-centered care to improve TB treatment outcomes and overall health. Globally, TB remains a significant cause of illness and death, driven by key health-related risk factors such as diabetes, HIV, smoking, undernutrition, and alcohol use disorders. These factors contribute to nearly half of all new TB cases worldwide. Additionally, individuals with TB often experience other comorbidities, including mental health conditions, pulmonary diseases, and viral hepatitis. These comorbidities can lead to poor treatment outcomes, reduced quality of life, and increased financial burdens. Addressing these issues is a critical component of the WHO's End TB Strategy, which aims to provide integrated care and prevention. The handbook highlights the need for routine assessment and management of TB-related comorbidities and risk factors to improve treatment outcomes. It aligns with the commitments made in the 2018 United Nations High-Level Meeting on TB, which emphasized a comprehensive response to TB, including addressing social and economic determinants and protecting human rights. The handbook also supports the integration of TB care with services for HIV, noncommunicable diseases, and mental health. Mental health conditions are particularly prevalent among individuals with TB, with nearly one billion people worldwide living with a mental disorder. TB patients are at higher risk for mental health conditions and substance use disorders, which can negatively impact their ability to adhere to treatment and infection control practices. Depression, anxiety, and psychosis are common among TB patients, and some anti-TB medications are associated with these conditions. Individuals with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) are at an even higher risk for mental health issues. Stigma and discrimination related to TB can further exacerbate mental health conditions and substance use disorders. The handbook emphasizes the importance of prevention, early identification, monitoring, and treatment of mental health conditions and substance use disorders in TB patients. It advocates for people-centered care, which includes social support, education, and access to psychological and material resources to mitigate the impact of poverty, stigma, and discrimination on mental health. Social protection interventions, such as financial and food security support, can help reduce stress and prevent mental health conditions. The integration of mental health care into TB services is a key component of the End TB Strategy. This includes identifying and managing mental health and substance use conditions in TB patients through referrals to specialized services or task-shifting to primary care health workers trained in mental health care. Screening tools for mental health and substance use disorders are available and can be used to identify individuals in need of further assessment and care. Ensuring referral pathways to mental health services and training non-specialist health workers in mental health care are essential steps to bridge the treatment gap and improve coverage for priority mental health conditions. The WHO has developed guidelines and tools, such as the Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), to support the management of mental health disorders in non-specialized settings. These resources provide evidence-based guidance for health professionals to identify, assess, manage, and follow up on mental health conditions in TB patients. The handbook also includes specific guidance for addressing substance use disorders and other mental health conditions in TB care settings. In summary, the WHO operational handbook on TB and comorbidities provides practical guidance for integrating mental health care into TB services. It aims to improve the quality of care for individuals with TB and comorbidities, reduce stigma and discrimination, and enhance health, social, and economic outcomes over the long term.
